extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, number theorists, and informed public following the abc conjecture / IUT controversy
extracted.subtask_description: A blog post discussing the dispute over Shinichi Mochizuki's claimed proof of the abc conjecture, the criticisms raised by Scholze and Stix, and norms of professional conduct and communication in mathematical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: It seemed best then to not publicize this here, better to give Mochizuki, Scholze and Stix the time to sort out the mathematics and wait for them to have something to say publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publicizing rumors or the existence/authorship of not-yet-public manuscripts until the involved parties have had a chance to sort out matters and make a public statement; give primary actors time to respond before broad public discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect collegial norms on announcing others' unpublished work
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a collegial standard of not publicly broadcasting mathematical work that the authors have not yet announced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publicly attribute or characterize an unpublished manuscript's authorship or conclusions before the authors have chosen to release it; doing so may breach professional norms even if journalism might treat it as 'fair game.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof lies with the claimant
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof is on Mochizuki — no matter how often he claims he has proven ABC, or no matter the loftiness of the terms in which he expounds the correct manner to become an 'expert' in his proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary claims require the claimant to provide convincing, checkable arguments and to make the proof accessible enough that independent experts can verify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public criticism must be concrete and evidence-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative online criticism went always in a very vague form without any single concrete mathematical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public critiques of mathematical work should present specific mathematical objections or evidence rather than vague, hostile or imprecise commentary; criticism without concrete evidence is poor practice and unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and revisability of manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: An author needs to be told to rewrite a manuscript since in its current form others cannot understand it or check it with some reasonable amount of effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be prepared to revise and clarify manuscripts so that competent peers can follow and check the arguments; a failure to make work reasonably comprehensible is a legitimate ground for asking for rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee responsibility to address substantive criticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The new twist to this story is that evidently Scholze long ago had specific criticisms of the proof, and that these never got answered by Mochizuki or addressed by the referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and editorial processes should engage with and respond to substantive criticisms raised by experts; ignoring concrete expert objections during review is a failure of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat expert questions seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Peter Scholze is by far the most talented arithmetic geometer of his generation... That his questions about Mochizuki’s proof were 'shallow' seems highly unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions and objections raised by leading domain experts should be taken seriously and investigated thoroughly rather than dismissed out of hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make assumptions explicit and avoid predicating arguments on unaccepted assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem in the dialogue occurs when one party starts making assumptions that the other party does not accept, and predicating their arguments on these assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics should state underlying assumptions clearly; failing to recognize or disclose assumptions undermines the argumentative exchange and can amount to intellectual malpractice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of direct (face-to-face) communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly because of the importance of face-to-face communication, Scholze and Stix traveled to Kyoto to talk to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof or theory is especially difficult to parse, direct conversations, seminars, and presentations can be crucial to resolving misunderstandings and should be used to facilitate checking and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate skepticism when work is hard to check
rubrics_metrics.description: There are quite good reasons for why experts have been skeptical about IUT and the supposed abc proof, reasons which will be conclusively vindicated if Scholze and Stix turn out to be right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism is a reasonable stance when a result is hard to verify; experts may withhold acceptance until specific problems are resolved and clear, checkable explanations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in accusing intellectual dishonesty
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t think 'intellectual dishonesty' is a good way to characterize the problem... I have no doubt Mochizuki was and is sincere in his belief that he both has a proof, and has written it down carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid labeling colleagues as intellectually dishonest based on inferred mental states; focus on observable behaviors (e.g., failure to respond to substantive criticisms, refusal to revise) and prefer concrete evidence when making such accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer private expert discussion before public denunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: It seemed best then to not publicize this here, better to give Mochizuki, Scholze and Stix the time to sort out the mathematics and wait for them to have something to say publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, experts should attempt to resolve technical disputes through private or expert channels first; public denunciation prior to such attempts can be premature and counterproductive.
